nikolaos-tselementes.name: Nikolaos Tselementes
nikolaos-tselementes.summary: Greek chef and cookbook author (1878–1958) specializing in Greek and French cuisine, considered one of modern Greece's most influential cookery writers.

ottoman-cuisine.name: Ottoman cuisine
ottoman-cuisine.summary: The cuisine of the Ottoman Empire, which continues today in the cooking of Turkey, the Balkans, the Caucasus, the Middle East and North Africa.

pirozhki.name: Pirozhki
pirozhki.summary: Baked or fried yeast-leavened buns with a variety of fillings, a popular street food in Russian and Eastern European cuisine.

pastitsio.name: Pastitsio
pastitsio.summary: A baked pasta dish with ground meat and béchamel sauce from Greece's Ionian Islands, with variations found elsewhere around the Mediterranean.

pontic-greek-cuisine.name: Pontic Greek cuisine
pontic-greek-cuisine.summary: The traditional food of the Pontic Greeks from the Black Sea's southern shore, shaped by neighboring Russian, Turkish, Laz, Hemshin and Armenian influences.

s-rmene.name: Sürmene (Sourmena)
s-rmene.summary: A district and municipality of Trabzon Province, Turkey, known in Greek as Sourmena; before 1923 it had a large Greek community of around 14,000 people.

ordu.name: Ordu
ordu.summary: A port city on Turkey's Black Sea coast and capital of Ordu Province, with a population of about 235,000 as of 2023.

koliva.name: Kollyva
koliva.summary: A dish of boiled wheat used in the Eastern Orthodox Church at funerals and memorial services for the dead.

national-gallery-athens.name: National Gallery (Athens)
national-gallery-athens.summary: Greece's national art museum in Athens, showing Greek and European art from the 14th to 20th centuries; it reopened in 2021 after an 8-year refurbishment.

demetrios-galanis.name: Demetrios Galanis
demetrios-galanis.summary: A Greek artist (1879-1966) and friend of Picasso who exhibited alongside Matisse, Braque and Chagall in Paris and became one of the most acclaimed Greek modern artists abroad.

acad-mie-fran-aise.name: Académie Française
acad-mie-fran-aise.summary: France's principal authority on the French language, established in 1635, made up of forty lifetime members who publish an official dictionary.

nikos-engonopoulos.name: Nikos Engonopoulos
nikos-engonopoulos.summary: Greek painter and poet (1907–1985), a leading figure of the 'Generation of the '30s' and a major representative of surrealism in Greece.

dimitris-mytaras.name: Dimitris Mytaras
dimitris-mytaras.summary: Greek painter (1934–2017) regarded as one of Greece's important 20th-century artists, whose work moved from naturalism toward an expressionistic style after 1975.

yiannis-psychopedis.name: Yiannis Psychopedis
yiannis-psychopedis.summary: Greek painter born in 1945, one of the country's main exponents of Critical Realism, an art movement that emerged after the upheavals of 1968.

konstantinos-parthenis.name: Konstantinos Parthenis
konstantinos-parthenis.summary: Greek painter (1878–1967) born in Alexandria who broke with 19th-century Greek academic tradition, introducing modern elements alongside traditional themes such as the figure of Christ.

konstantinos-maleas.name: Konstantinos Maleas
konstantinos-maleas.summary: Post-Impressionist Greek painter (1879–1928), regarded alongside Konstantinos Parthenis as one of Greece's most important modern artists.

national-glyptotheque.name: National Glyptotheque
national-glyptotheque.summary: A sculpture museum in Athens, an annex of the National Gallery of Greece, established in 2004 to house Greek sculpture from the 19th and 20th centuries.

provisional-democratic-government.name: Provisional Democratic Government of Greece
provisional-democratic-government.summary: The communist administration declared in Greece in December 1947 during the Greek Civil War, controlling northern mountain areas and backed by the USSR and Eastern Bloc.

benito-mussolini.name: Benito Mussolini
benito-mussolini.summary: Italian dictator (1883–1945) who founded fascism and led Italy from 1922 until his overthrow in 1943; executed by the Italian resistance in 1945.

ioannis-metaxas.name: Ioannis Metaxas
ioannis-metaxas.summary: Greek general and dictator of Greece from 1936 until his death in 1941, who established an authoritarian, anti-communist regime after a self-coup.

hellenic-army.name: Hellenic Army
hellenic-army.summary: The land force of Greece, formed in 1828 and the largest branch of the Hellenic Armed Forces.

battle-of-crete.name: Battle of Crete
battle-of-crete.summary: A 1941 German airborne and amphibious invasion of Crete, the first large-scale airborne invasion in history, forcing Allied troops to evacuate or surrender after heavy fighting.

constantine-i-of-greece.name: Constantine I of Greece
constantine-i-of-greece.summary: King of Greece (1913–1917, 1920–1922) whose pro-German stance during World War I caused the National Schism, splitting the country.

eleftherios-venizelos.name: Eleftherios Venizelos
eleftherios-venizelos.summary: Greek statesman who served as prime minister for over 12 years between 1910 and 1933, leading reforms and helping Greece expand after the Balkan Wars.

national-schism.name: National Schism
national-schism.summary: Series of disputes from 1915 to 1922 between King Constantine I and Prime Minister Eleftherios Venizelos over whether Greece should join World War I, splitting the country into rival governments.

gavrilo-princip.name: Gavrilo Princip
gavrilo-princip.summary: Bosnian Serb student (1894–1918) who assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo in 1914, setting off the crisis that led to World War I.

archduke-franz-ferdinand-of-austria.name: Archduke Franz Ferdinand
archduke-franz-ferdinand-of-austria.summary: Heir presumptive to the Austro-Hungarian throne (1863–1914) whose assassination in Sarajevo by Gavrilo Princip triggered the chain of events leading to World War I.

macedonian-front.name: Macedonian front
macedonian-front.summary: World War I theatre, also called the Salonica front, where Allied forces aided Serbia against Germany, Austria-Hungary and Bulgaria from 1915 until victory in 1918.

battle-of-skra-di-legen.name: Battle of Skra-di-Legen
battle-of-skra-di-legen.summary: A two-day 1918 World War I battle on the Macedonian front in which Greek and French forces captured heavily fortified Bulgarian positions, the first large-scale action of Greek troops on that front.

louis-franchet-d-esp-rey.name: Louis Franchet d'Espèrey
louis-franchet-d-esp-rey.summary: A French general in World War I who helped organize the Allied response at the First Battle of the Marne in 1914 and later led the successful Macedonian campaign.

4th-of-august-regime.name: 4th of August Regime
4th-of-august-regime.summary: A dictatorial, ultranationalist government led by General Ioannis Metaxas that ruled Greece from 1936 until the German invasion in 1941, backed by King George II.

metaxas-line.name: Metaxas Line
metaxas-line.summary: A chain of Greek border fortifications built to guard against a Bulgarian invasion, named after Prime Minister Ioannis Metaxas and made up of 21 fortified complexes with tunnels and gun emplacements.

democratic-army-of-greece.name: Democratic Army of Greece
democratic-army-of-greece.summary: The army founded by the Communist Party of Greece in 1946 that fought for the Provisional Democratic Government in the Greek Civil War, reaching about 50,000 fighters at its peak.

alexandros-papagos.name: Alexandros Papagos
alexandros-papagos.summary: A Greek military officer and Field Marshal (1883–1955) who led the Hellenic Army in World War II, later serving as Prime Minister of Greece from 1952 to 1955.

wehrmacht.name: Wehrmacht
wehrmacht.summary: The unified armed forces of Nazi Germany from 1935 to 1945, combining the army, navy and air force, central to Germany's power in World War II.

117th-j-ger-division.name: 117th Jäger Division
117th-j-ger-division.summary: German infantry division of World War II, formed in 1943 from an earlier unit; it served in the Balkans on anti-partisan duty before ending the war fighting on the Eastern Front.

kalavryta.name: Kalavryta
kalavryta.summary: A mountain town in Achaea, Greece, whose entire male population was killed and the town destroyed by German occupation troops in December 1943.

greek-ship-elli.name: Greek cruiser Elli
greek-ship-elli.summary: A Greek protected cruiser in service from 1914, sunk by an Italian submarine on 15 August 1940, an incident that helped trigger the Greco-Italian War.

elas.name: ELAS
elas.summary: The Greek People's Liberation Army, the largest Greek resistance force against Axis occupation during World War II, linked to the Communist Party of Greece and disbanded in 1945.

gyaros.name: Gyaros
gyaros.summary: A small, largely uninhabited Greek island used as a place of exile in the early Roman Empire and later as a prison island for political dissidents from 1948 to 1974.

makronisos.name: Makronisos
makronisos.summary: Greek Aegean island, the largest uninhabited one in Greece, notorious as a political prison from the 1920s to the 1970s.

epirus-region.name: Epirus
epirus-region.summary: A geographic and administrative region in northwestern Greece bordering Albania, part of a wider historical region straddling modern Albania and Greece.

t-a-obreht.name: Téa Obreht
t-a-obreht.summary: American novelist born in 1985 who won the 2011 Orange Prize for Fiction for her debut novel, The Tiger's Wife.

the-tiger-s-wife.name: The Tiger's Wife
the-tiger-s-wife.summary: Téa Obreht's 2011 debut novel, set in the mid-20th to early 21st-century Balkans, exploring generations of a medical family through several wars; it won the Orange Prize for Fiction, making Obreht, at 25, the youngest winner ever.

women-s-prize-for-fiction.name: Orange Prize for Fiction
women-s-prize-for-fiction.summary: A prestigious UK literary prize for a female author's best novel in English, known under this name from 1996 to 2006 and 2009 to 2012.

national-book-award-for-fiction.name: National Book Award for Fiction
national-book-award-for-fiction.summary: One of the five annual U.S. National Book Awards, honoring outstanding fiction by American citizens; judged by fellow writers and administered by the National Book Foundation since 1987.

dylan-thomas-prize.name: Dylan Thomas Prize
dylan-thomas-prize.summary: An annual literary prize for published writers under forty writing in English, named after the poet Dylan Thomas and worth £30,000, awarded across genres including poetry, fiction and drama.

alice-munro.name: Alice Munro
alice-munro.summary: Canadian short story writer (1931–2024) awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2013, known for stories set in rural Ontario and a meticulous, simple prose style.

charles-simic.name: Charles Simic
charles-simic.summary: Serbian American poet (1938–2023) who won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry in 1990 and later served as U.S. Poet Laureate from 2007.

mikhail-bulgakov.name: Mikhail Bulgakov
mikhail-bulgakov.summary: Russian and Soviet novelist and playwright (1891–1940) whose posthumously published novel The Master and Margarita is considered a masterpiece; some of his works were banned by Stalin's government.

gabriel-garc-a-m-rquez.name: Gabriel García Márquez
gabriel-garc-a-m-rquez.summary: Colombian writer and journalist (1927–2014), awarded the 1982 Nobel Prize in Literature and known for popularizing magic realism in novels like One Hundred Years of Solitude.

milorad-pavi.name: Milorad Pavić
milorad-pavi.summary: Serbian writer and academic (1929–2009) best known for his 1984 novel Dictionary of the Khazars, hailed as 'the first novel of the 21st century' and popular across Europe and South America.

dictionary-of-the-khazars.name: Dictionary of the Khazars
dictionary-of-the-khazars.summary: 1984 debut novel by Serbian writer Milorad Pavić, written as a lexicon with no conventional plot, centered on the historical conversion of the Khazar people to monotheism.

miltos-sachtouris.name: Miltos Sachtouris
miltos-sachtouris.summary: Greek poet (1919–2005) who abandoned law studies for poetry, writing under the pen name Miltos Chrysanthis and publishing his first collection in 1941.

eleni-vakalo.name: Eleni Vakalo
eleni-vakalo.summary: A Greek poet, art critic and art historian who lived from 1921 to 2001.

nanos-valaoritis.name: Nanos Valaoritis
nanos-valaoritis.summary: Greek writer (1921–2019), published as poet, novelist and playwright since 1939, regarded as the most important poet of the Greek diaspora since Cavafy.

katerina-gogou.name: Katerina Gogou
katerina-gogou.summary: A Greek poet, author and actress (1940–1993).

manolis-pratikakis.name: Manolis Pratikakis
manolis-pratikakis.summary: A Greek poet born in 1943 and a practicing neurologist and psychiatrist, part of Greece's 1970s Generation of poets; he won the Greek National Book Award in 2003.

argyris-chionis.name: Argyris Chionis
argyris-chionis.summary: Greek poet (1943–2011) who emigrated to Paris shortly after the military junta seized power in Greece in 1967.

yannis-kondos.name: Yannis Kondos
yannis-kondos.summary: Greek poet (1943–2015) of the '1970s Generation', awarded the State Prize for Poetry in 1998 for his collection Absurd Athlete.

pavlos-matesis.name: Pavlos Matesis
pavlos-matesis.summary: A Greek novelist, playwright and translator, 1933 to 2013, best known for his acclaimed novel The Daughter.

first-balkan-war.name: First Balkan War
first-balkan-war.summary: War fought October 1912 to May 1913 in which the Balkan League (Bulgaria, Serbia, Greece, Montenegro) defeated the Ottoman Empire, stripping it of most of its European territory.

balkan-league.name: Balkan League
balkan-league.summary: A 1912 alliance of Greece, Bulgaria, Serbia and Montenegro against the Ottoman Empire, spearheaded by Eleftherios Venizelos; its First Balkan War victory was followed by a split among the allies.

east-thrace.name: Eastern Thrace
east-thrace.summary: The part of Turkey geographically in Southeast Europe, separated from Anatolia by the Dardanelles, Sea of Marmara and Bosphorus, and including part of Istanbul.

july-crisis.name: July Crisis
july-crisis.summary: The chain of diplomatic and military escalations among European powers in mid-1914, beginning with the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, that led to the outbreak of World War I.

greco-italian-war.name: Greco-Italian War
greco-italian-war.summary: A 1940 to 1941 war begun by Italy's invasion of Greece from Albania; Greek forces repelled the Italians, dealing the Axis its first major setback of World War II.

second-balkan-war.name: Second Balkan War
second-balkan-war.summary: An 1913 conflict in which Bulgaria fought its former Balkan League allies plus Romania and the Ottoman Empire over Macedonia, ending with Bulgaria ceding territory under the Treaty of Bucharest.

treaty-of-bucharest-1913.name: Treaty of Bucharest (1913)
treaty-of-bucharest-1913.summary: Signed in August 1913 by Bulgaria, Romania, Serbia, Montenegro and Greece, it amended the earlier Treaty of London and ended the Second Balkan War.

dobruja.name: Dobruja
dobruja.summary: A region in Southeastern Europe between the lower Danube River and the Black Sea, divided between Romania and Bulgaria since the 19th century.

greek-genocide.name: Greek genocide
greek-genocide.summary: The systematic killing of Christian Ottoman Greeks in Anatolia between 1912 and 1923, carried out through massacres, death marches and expulsions by Ottoman and Turkish nationalist forces.

population-exchange-between-greece-and-t.name: Greek–Turkish population exchange
population-exchange-between-greece-and-t.summary: The 1923 mass expulsion of over a million Greek Orthodox Christians from Turkey and hundreds of thousands of Muslims from Greece, agreed at Lausanne to normalize relations after the Greco-Turkish War.
population-exchange-between-greece-and-t.source_title: Population exchange between Greece and Turkey

pontic-greek-genocide.name: Pontic Greek genocide
pontic-greek-genocide.summary: The systematic destruction of the Greek community in Turkey's Pontus region during and after World War I, carried out first under the Committee of Union and Progress and then the Kemalist regime.

committee-of-union-and-progress.name: Committee of Union and Progress
committee-of-union-and-progress.summary: An Ottoman revolutionary group, secret society and political party active from 1889 to 1926, associated with the 'Young Turks', that forced restoration of the 1876 constitution in 1908.

three-pashas.name: Three Pashas
three-pashas.summary: The triumvirate of Ottoman leaders, Talaat, Enver and Djemal Pasha, who ruled the empire after 1913, led it into World War I, and were responsible for the Armenian genocide.

kemalism.name: Kemalism
kemalism.summary: The political ideology of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, founder of Turkey, marked by secularizing and modernizing reforms that separated the new republic from its Ottoman predecessor.

slobodan-milo-evi.name: Slobodan Milošević
slobodan-milo-evi.summary: Serbian and Yugoslav politician who was Serbia's president from 1989 to 1997 and Yugoslavia's from 1997 to 2000, later the first sitting head of state charged with war crimes.

international-criminal-tribunal-for-the-.name: International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia
international-criminal-tribunal-for-the-.summary: A United Nations court in The Hague, operating from 1993 to 2017, established to prosecute war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity committed during the Yugoslav Wars.
international-criminal-tribunal-for-the-.source_title: International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia

yugoslav-wars.name: Yugoslav Wars
yugoslav-wars.summary: A series of ethnic conflicts and wars of independence from 1991 to 2001 that accompanied the breakup of Yugoslavia into six countries.

greek-civil-war.name: Greek Civil War
greek-civil-war.summary: A 1946 to 1949 conflict between Communist-led rebels and the Greek royal government, which prevailed with British and American support.

eastern-bloc.name: Eastern Bloc
eastern-bloc.summary: An unofficial coalition of Soviet-aligned communist states across Central and Eastern Europe and beyond, existing through the Cold War from 1947 to 1991.

pontic-greeks.name: Pontic Greeks
pontic-greeks.summary: An ethnically Greek people indigenous to the Pontus region of northeastern Anatolia, with their own language, cuisine, music and dance, largely resettled in Greece after 1923.

caucasus-greeks.name: Caucasus Greeks
caucasus-greeks.summary: Ethnic Greeks of the North Caucasus and Transcaucasia, whose migration into the region predates the Christian era, with most communities dating from the late Ottoman period.

hellenism-modern-religion.name: Hellenism (modern religion)
hellenism-modern-religion.summary: A modern neopagan religion reviving worship of the ancient Greek gods through prayer and festivals; organized movements emerged in Greece in the 1990s and it was legally recognized there in 2017.

eusebeia.name: Eusebeia
eusebeia.summary: A Greek word meaning piety or reverence toward the gods, used in Greek philosophy and in Greek translations of religious texts, including the New Testament.

arete.name: Arete
arete.summary: An ancient Greek concept meaning excellence or the full realization of a person's or thing's potential, sometimes personified as a minor goddess.

xenia-greek.name: Xenia
xenia-greek.summary: An ancient Greek concept of hospitality toward strangers, rooted in gift exchange and reciprocity, treated as both a moral duty and a political imperative, honoring Zeus Xenios.

stathis-psillos.name: Stathis Psillos
stathis-psillos.summary: A Greek philosopher of science, professor at the University of Athens, ranked among the most cited living philosophers in 2015.

to-vima.name: To Vima
to-vima.summary: A Greek weekly newspaper founded in 1922, one of Greece's major publications, with an English-language international edition.

atheist-union-of-greece.name: Atheist Union of Greece
atheist-union-of-greece.summary: Nonprofit organization based in Athens, founded in 2010, that defends the rights of Greek atheists and advocates for separation of church and state.

david-papineau.name: David Papineau
david-papineau.summary: A British academic philosopher, born in 1947, who works as Professor of Philosophy of Science at King's College London and previously taught at Cambridge.

ellinais.name: Ellinais
ellinais.summary: An Athens-based organization founded in 2005 to promote Hellenismos, the modern revival of worship of the ancient Greek gods, with official state recognition.

temple-of-olympian-zeus-athens.name: Temple of Olympian Zeus
temple-of-olympian-zeus-athens.summary: A colossal Athens temple to Zeus begun in the 6th century BC but not finished until Emperor Hadrian's reign, once holding 104 columns and one of the largest cult statues in the ancient world.

council-of-state-greece.name: Council of State (Greece)
council-of-state-greece.summary: Greece's supreme court for administrative law, handling matters other than public finance, which is overseen separately by the Court of Audit.

john-worrall-philosopher.name: John Worrall
john-worrall-philosopher.summary: British philosopher of science (born 1946) who was a professor of philosophy of science at the London School of Economics until retiring in 2019.

martin-curd.name: Martin Curd
martin-curd.summary: American philosopher and associate professor at Purdue University known for his work on the philosophy of science.

british-journal-for-the-philosophy-of-sc.name: British Journal for the Philosophy of Science
british-journal-for-the-philosophy-of-sc.summary: Peer-reviewed academic philosophy journal, owned by the British Society for the Philosophy of Science and published by the University of Chicago Press.
british-journal-for-the-philosophy-of-sc.source_title: British Journal for the Philosophy of Science

metascience-journal.name: Metascience (journal)
metascience-journal.summary: A peer-reviewed academic journal, founded in 1984, that publishes book reviews in the history and philosophy of science.

academia-europaea.name: Academia Europaea
academia-europaea.summary: A pan-European scientific association founded in 1988 covering all fields of scholarship and coordinating European research interests.

michael-cacoyannis.name: Michael Cacoyannis
michael-cacoyannis.summary: A Cypriot and Greek filmmaker (1921–2011) best known for directing Zorba the Greek, earning five Academy Award nominations, more than any other Cypriot.

melina-mercouri.name: Melina Mercouri
melina-mercouri.summary: A Greek actress, singer and politician (1920–1994) who won acting awards including at Cannes, then became Greece's first female Minister of Culture and campaigned for the return of the Parthenon Marbles.

irene-papas.name: Irene Papas
irene-papas.summary: Greek actress and singer (1929-2022) who starred in over 70 films across more than 50 years, gaining international recognition for The Guns of Navarone, Zorba the Greek and Z.

serra-dance.name: Serra
serra-dance.summary: A communal, recreational Pontic Greek folk dance performed at festivities and named after the Sera river valley; no real evidence links it to the ancient Pyrrhic war dance.

kemen-e-of-the-black-sea.name: Pontic lyra
kemen-e-of-the-black-sea.summary: A traditional three-stringed bowed instrument played by Turkish and Greek folk musicians from the Black Sea region.

stella-1955-film.name: Stella (1955 film)
stella-1955-film.summary: A 1955 Greek film retelling Carmen, starring Melina Mercouri and directed by Michael Cacoyannis; initially controversial, it is now ranked among the greatest Greek films.

iakovos-kambanellis.name: Iakovos Kambanellis
iakovos-kambanellis.summary: A Greek poet, playwright, screenwriter, lyricist and novelist (1921–2011).

zorba-the-greek-film.name: Zorba the Greek
zorba-the-greek-film.summary: A 1964 Greek film directed by Michael Cacoyannis, starring Anthony Quinn as a boisterous Cretan peasant, based on Nikos Kazantzakis's 1946 novel.

anthony-quinn.name: Anthony Quinn
anthony-quinn.summary: Mexican and American actor (1915–2001) known for portraying passionate, earthy characters in over 100 films; won two Academy Awards, including for Viva Zapata! and Lust for Life.

theo-angelopoulos.name: Theo Angelopoulos
theo-angelopoulos.summary: Greek filmmaker (1935–2012) known for slow, hypnotic long takes; his film Eternity and a Day won the Palme d'Or at Cannes in 1998.

eternity-and-a-day.name: Eternity and a Day
eternity-and-a-day.summary: A 1998 Greek drama film directed by Theo Angelopoulos that won the Palme d'Or at the Cannes Film Festival.

palme-d-or.name: Palme d'Or
palme-d-or.summary: The top prize awarded to the director of the best film at the Cannes Film Festival, introduced in 1955 and considered one of the film industry's most prestigious honors.

prize-of-the-ecumenical-jury.name: Prize of the Ecumenical Jury
prize-of-the-ecumenical-jury.summary: An independent film award given since 1973 by Christian juries at major festivals such as Cannes, honoring works that reveal the depths of human hopes and struggles.

pontic-greek.name: Romeika
pontic-greek.summary: The traditional native name for Pontic Greek, an endangered language variety spoken by descendants of Greek communities from the Black Sea's southern shore.

apolas-lermi.name: Apolas Lermi
apolas-lermi.summary: The stage name of Abdurrahman Lermi (born 1986), a Turkish folk singer and musician.

trabzon.name: Trabzon
trabzon.summary: City on Turkey's Black Sea coast, founded in 756 BC by Greek colonists, later capital of the Byzantine successor Empire of Trebizond before falling to the Ottomans in 1461.

greece_balkans-modern-science-007: British Journal for the Philosophy of Science
